content: The 2012 UNAIDS Global Report on the AIDS epidemic provides a comprehensive analysis of the global HIV/AIDS situation, including epidemiological data, trends, and progress in combating the epidemic. The 2013 UNAIDS Global Report further elaborates on these findings, offering updated statistics and insights into the effectiveness of interventions. The 2014 UNAIDS Progress Report on the Global Plan focuses on the implementation of strategies to eliminate new HIV infections among children and ensure the health and survival of mothers living with HIV. The 2012 UNICEF report emphasizes the importance of implementing equity-focused approaches, such as Options B and B+, to prevent mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) of HIV and to maintain the health of mothers. These approaches involve initiating lifelong antiretroviral therapy (ART) for pregnant women living with HIV, regardless of their CD4 count, to reduce transmission risks and improve maternal health outcomes. Van Lettow et al. (2014) evaluated the performance of different care models for initiating lifelong ART in pregnant women in Malawi under the Option B+ strategy. Their findings highlight the effectiveness of this approach in reducing mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HIV and improving maternal health outcomes. The 2010 WHO guidelines recommend a public health approach to ART for adults and adolescents living with HIV, while the 2012 WHO programmatic update focuses on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating pregnant women and preventing HIV transmission to infants. The 2013 WHO consolidated guidelines provide comprehensive recommendations on the use of antiretroviral drugs for both treatment and prevention of HIV infection. Studies on Option B and Option B+ have demonstrated varying levels of success in reducing MTCT rates and improving maternal and infant health outcomes. For example, Lingui et al. (2012) reported a 4% MTCT rate at 12 months in Côte d’Ivoire, while other studies have shown the benefits of early ART initiation and adherence in reducing transmission risks. The Kesho Bora study group (2012) found that triple antiretroviral prophylaxis significantly reduced the risk of MTCT compared to standard regimens, without increasing adverse events in mothers or infants. Similarly, the Kisumu Breastfeeding Study (2014) demonstrated the benefits of maternal ART during breastfeeding in reducing postnatal HIV transmission. Retention in care and adherence to ART remain critical challenges, as highlighted by studies such as Phillips et al. (2014) and Tweya et al. (2014). These studies emphasize the need for strategies to improve retention and adherence, particularly during the postpartum period, to ensure sustained viral suppression and prevent transmission. The systematic review and meta-analysis by Fonner et al. (2015) evaluated the effectiveness and safety of oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for HIV prevention across diverse populations. The findings support the use of PrEP as an additional prevention option, with evidence of efficacy in reducing HIV infection risk and minimal adverse effects. Overall, these studies and reports underscore the importance of comprehensive, evidence-based strategies to prevent HIV transmission, improve maternal and infant health outcomes, and address barriers to care and treatment adherence.
